doc.title: Mickey Roker interviewed by Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 31, 1995

title: Music as an expression of life: Gospel, significant tone, emotional truth
summary: Roker says authentic music comes from living with the people, like Gospel from poor people, and discusses emotional truth with Woods.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: You mentioned earlier on in our talk about the Gospel influence. Tell us how that finds its way into the music. And I want to mention a term here, and then you take off on it. There’s a term that deals with several West African languages, called significant tone. And that means that the way that you pronounce a word, whether you give a higher inflection or a lower inflection to that tone, actually changes the meaning of the tone. And then of course I teach in my courses that when people came here from West Africa, and you play on a saxophone or a trumpet but your language was one that used significant tone, you’re still trying to get those inflections out of that inanimate piece of metal. Make that thing speak and give you the sound that you want back.

Well see you have to, like let’s say you want to play Latin music. You cannot play Latin music until you live and, I mean you can play it but you won’t be authentic. Just like we might learn French. We might go to school and learn how to speak French. But you won’t speak French until you go to France and live in France. See music is an expression of life. You see? So you have to live, you’ve got to live and be with people to be able to express how they feel musically. Because the music comes from the people, the soul people or poor people or the soul of the music, like the Gospel. It comes from the poor people. The poor people of America, the people who have been abused, the people who have a lot to cry about and rejoice about. You see? So that’s you know, expression comes from people. And the music comes from the people. You understand what I’m saying?

There’s a thing I want to ask you about, and this is a term that I use and let’s see how you feel about it, a thing that I call emotional truth. Now I explained it like this. I said there is truth, which we call just fact, and then there’s emotional truth. Now we all know that there was a Vietnam War. That’s a fact. That is true. But if you’re talking to a mother who lost her son in that war, and she breaks down and cry while you’re talking to her, now that’s the emotional truth.

Well it’s like looking at a picture. Some people look at a picture and they see something completely different. You know what I mean? You know if a mother lost her son, she’d look at a picture of the Vietnam War man, she’s going to be affected quite differently © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
than some guy that was a soldier and got a medal for it. You know what I’m saying? So that’s what that is you know.
